exam2.explanation: A phased array has a small footprint and steers the beam electronically, so it can image between ribs, which is why it is used for cardiac work. Its near-field resolution is relatively poor.
exam2.hint: Consider why this probe is the standard for scanning the heart through rib spaces.

exam2.question: In 2D image, which adjustment would sharpen the borders of a structure?
exam2.explanation: Edge enhancement is a processing function that accentuates boundaries to make margins appear sharper. Increasing dynamic range smooths the image and softens borders.
exam2.hint: One processing control is designed specifically to accentuate boundaries.

exam2.question: What occurs when the sound beam interacts with normal incidence at nonspecular reflector?
exam2.explanation: Nonspecular reflectors are rough or smaller than the wavelength, so they redirect sound in many directions, which is scattering. Refraction requires oblique incidence and a change in speed.
exam2.hint: Rough or tiny reflectors redirect sound in many directions regardless of incidence.

exam2.question: Which factor determines elevational resolution?
exam2.explanation: Elevational resolution is determined by the thickness of the beam perpendicular to the scan plane (slice thickness). Beam width in the scan plane determines lateral resolution.
exam2.hint: Elevational refers to the dimension perpendicular to the imaging plane.

exam2.question: What resolution is this image depicting?
exam2.explanation: The phantom pins are arranged one above another along the beam direction with decreasing spacing, which tests axial resolution. Lateral resolution pins are arranged side by side, perpendicular to the beam.
exam2.hint: Notice the orientation of the closely spaced pins relative to the direction of the beam.
exam2.imageCaption: Phantom image showing a group of pin targets

exam2.question: Which factor decreases when output is reduced?
exam2.explanation: Reducing output power lowers the voltage driving the crystal, decreasing the pressure amplitude (and intensity) of the transmitted wave. Frequency and PRF are independent of output power.
exam2.hint: Output power controls the strength of the pulse, not its timing or frequency.

exam2.question: What can be increased to eliminate clutter from color flow imaging?
exam2.explanation: Clutter is low-velocity, high-amplitude signal from moving tissue, which the wall filter removes. Increasing color gain would add more noise.
exam2.hint: Clutter comes from slow tissue motion, which a high-pass filter rejects.

exam2.question: Which scanning position results in decreased blood flow to the sonographer shoulder/muscle/tendons?
exam2.explanation: Sustained arm abduction compresses the shoulder structures and reduces blood flow to the rotator cuff tendons, leading to shoulder injury. Excessive grip mainly stresses the hand and wrist.
exam2.hint: Think of the arm position that raises the elbow away from the body for long periods.

exam2.question: What improves both axial and lateral resolution?
exam2.explanation: Higher frequency shortens wavelength and spatial pulse length (better axial) and lessens divergence for a narrower far-field beam (better lateral). Reduced SPL alone improves only axial resolution.
exam2.hint: Find the single change that shortens wavelength and narrows the far field.

exam2.question: What determines shades of gray in B-mode imaging?
exam2.explanation: In brightness mode, the strength of each returning echo is converted into a pixel brightness level. PRF affects timing and frame rate, not brightness.
exam2.hint: B in B-mode stands for brightness, which is assigned from a property of each echo.

exam2.question: What is determined from the firing sequence of each element?
exam2.explanation: In an electronic array the timing pattern of element firing sets where the beam converges, so it determines the focal depth (and steering). Wavelength depends on frequency and medium, not on firing sequence.
exam2.hint: Electronic focusing relies on the relative timing of element excitation.

exam2.question: Where are harmonics created?
exam2.explanation: Tissue harmonics are generated within the tissue as the wave propagates nonlinearly. The signal processor only filters and processes them; it does not create them.
exam2.hint: Harmonic energy builds up as the wave travels deeper into the body.

exam2.question: Which type of resolution can be distorted with use of persistence?
exam2.explanation: Persistence averages several frames, so rapidly moving structures blur and the display lags behind real motion, degrading temporal resolution. Axial and lateral resolution are set by the pulse and beam, not by frame averaging.
exam2.hint: Frame averaging affects how faithfully motion is displayed over time.

exam2.question: Which factor influences acoustic impedance in a medium?
exam2.explanation: Acoustic impedance equals density times propagation speed, so density appears directly in the formula. Beam intensity has no effect on impedance; elasticity influences impedance only indirectly through speed.
exam2.hint: Write out the formula for acoustic impedance.

exam2.question: Which feature is a characteristic of CW Doppler?
exam2.explanation: CW Doppler needs at least two crystals, one continuously transmitting and one continuously receiving. It lacks range specificity and does not alias.
exam2.hint: A continuous system cannot send and listen with the same crystal at once.

exam2.question: Which parameter change does not increase frame rate?
exam2.explanation: A wider sector requires more scan lines per frame, which lowers frame rate. Decreasing depth and decreasing line density both raise frame rate.
exam2.hint: Frame rate falls when each frame needs more scan lines or deeper listening time.

exam2.question: How can the spectral Doppler mirroring seen in this image be eliminated?
exam2.explanation: Spectral mirroring is commonly caused by excessive Doppler gain, so lowering gain removes the false duplicate below the baseline. Increasing PRF corrects aliasing, not mirroring.
exam2.hint: Mirroring often appears when the Doppler receiver is overamplified.
exam2.imageCaption: Spectral Doppler waveform with signal on both sides of the baseline

exam2.question: Which color control adjustment caused the change in image A to become image B?
exam2.explanation: The color scale drops from 24 to 6, so the lower Nyquist limit makes the flow alias into mixed colors in image B. Changing the map would alter colors without changing the scale values.
exam2.hint: Compare the numbers at the top of the color bars in A and B.
exam2.imageCaption: Two color Doppler images of a vessel labeled A and B

exam3.question: Which artifact is seen as a result of an increased echo amplitude in the tissue located distal to an anechoic structure?
exam3.explanation: Sound passing through a weakly attenuating, fluid-filled structure arrives at deeper tissue with more energy, so those echoes are brighter (posterior enhancement). Reverberation produces equally spaced repeating lines, not a general brightening behind fluid.
exam3.hint: Think about what happens to beam energy after it crosses a fluid-filled structure that attenuates very little.

exam3.question: What improves axial resolution?
exam3.explanation: Axial resolution equals SPL/2, and SPL is the wavelength times the number of cycles; higher frequency means shorter wavelength and shorter SPL. Every listed option therefore improves axial resolution, so picking only one is incomplete.
exam3.hint: Recall the formula for axial resolution and which quantities make it up.

exam3.question: What is the primary purpose of backing material?

options.text: Increase a number of cycles in a pulse

exam3.explanation: Backing (damping) material shortens ringing, reducing the number of cycles per pulse, which shortens SPL and improves axial resolution. It decreases, not increases, the cycles in a pulse.
exam3.hint: Consider what damping does to the ringing of the crystal after it is excited.

exam3.question: Which control determines the amount of amplification occurring in the receiver?
exam3.explanation: Overall (receiver) gain amplifies all returning signals equally in the receiver. Output power changes the transmitted pulse strength, not receiver amplification.
exam3.hint: Separate the controls that act on the transmitted pulse from those that act on returning echoes.

exam3.question: Which action may reduce the number of lines in a frame without a loss of temporal resolution?
exam3.explanation: Narrowing the sector or field of view requires fewer scan lines per frame while keeping line density, so frame rate is maintained or improved. Decreasing depth shortens time per line but does not change the number of lines.
exam3.hint: Ask which control changes how many scan lines are needed to cover the image width.
keywords: number of lines in a frame

exam3.question: Which resolution is degraded when utilizing multiple focal zones?
exam3.explanation: Each focal zone needs its own pulse down every scan line, so more focal zones lower the frame rate and degrade temporal resolution. Lateral resolution actually improves over a longer region with multiple foci.
exam3.hint: Consider how many pulses per scan line are required when more focal zones are added.

exam3.question: What does changing the display depth control directly affect?
exam3.explanation: Deeper imaging requires a longer listening time between pulses, so PRP increases and PRF decreases. Pulse duration depends on the number of cycles and period, which the sonographer cannot change with the depth control.
exam3.hint: Think about how long the system must wait for echoes to return before sending the next pulse.

exam3.question: What is a potential negative consequence of using a high wall filter?

options.text: Too much noise may appear on the image

exam3.explanation: A wall filter rejects low-frequency Doppler shifts; set too high it removes real low-velocity blood flow signals. It has no effect on aliasing, which depends on PRF versus Doppler shift.
exam3.hint: Recall which frequencies a wall filter removes and what genuine flow lives in that range.

exam3.question: Which technique averages individual frames together to improve the images?
exam3.explanation: Persistence (frame averaging) combines consecutive frames to smooth noise and produce a smoother image. Compression changes the range of displayed amplitudes within a single frame.
exam3.hint: Look for the process that combines information from successive frames over time.

exam3.question: What produces increased attenuation within soft tissue?

options.text: Higher intensity of the ultrasound beam

exam3.explanation: Attenuation in soft tissue is about 0.5 dB/cm/MHz, so it rises with frequency and path length. Beam intensity does not change the attenuation coefficient.
exam3.hint: Recall the attenuation coefficient rule of thumb for soft tissue.

exam3.question: What relates bandwidth to operating frequency?
exam3.explanation: Quality factor (Q) equals operating (main) frequency divided by bandwidth; imaging transducers have low Q. The Nyquist limit relates PRF to the maximum detectable Doppler shift.
exam3.hint: Find the unitless number that describes how wide or narrow a transducer's frequency range is.

exam3.question: What improves the temporal resolution of color flow imaging?

options.text: Decreasing width of the color field of view

exam3.explanation: A narrower color box requires fewer color scan lines, each of which needs a full packet of pulses, so frame rate rises. Increasing ensemble length and lowering PRF both lengthen the time per frame.
exam3.hint: Color lines are the most time-consuming part of the frame; consider how to need fewer of them.
keywords: temporal resolution of color flow imaging

exam3.question: What is the term for the change in direction of a sound wave crossing a tissue boundary at an oblique angle?
exam3.explanation: Refraction is the bending of transmitted sound at an oblique boundary between media with different propagation speeds (Snell's law). Reflection is sound returning toward the source, not a change in the transmitted path.
exam3.hint: Recall the law that relates incident and transmitted angles to the propagation speeds of two media.

exam3.question: Which adjustment can maintain the same frame rate when the depth is increased?
exam3.explanation: Greater depth lengthens time per line; reducing image width lowers the number of lines per frame and offsets that time. More focal zones would reduce frame rate further, and frequency does not change frame rate.
exam3.hint: Frame time equals lines per frame times time per line; balance the increase in one with the other.

exam3.question: How is the intensity of an ultrasound beam measured?
exam3.explanation: A hydrophone is a small piezoelectric probe placed in a water tank to measure pressure, from which intensity and output values are derived. Autocorrelation is the processing method for color Doppler.
exam3.hint: Think of the small water-tank sensor used for acoustic output measurements.

exam3.question: Which component of a contrast agent causes a marked mismatch in impedance between the tissue?
exam3.explanation: Microbubble contrast agents contain gas, whose acoustic impedance is far lower than soft tissue, producing strong reflections. Liquids have impedances close to tissue and reflect weakly.
exam3.hint: Consider which state of matter has an acoustic impedance most different from soft tissue.

exam3.question: What can be increased to correct clutter artifact when using PW?
exam3.explanation: Clutter is low-frequency, high-amplitude signal from moving vessel walls or tissue, which the wall filter removes. Increasing Doppler gain would make clutter more prominent.
exam3.hint: Clutter comes from slow-moving, strongly reflecting tissue; pick the control that rejects low-frequency shifts.

exam3.question: Which machine setting could cause aliasing to occur?
exam3.explanation: The scale sets PRF, and the Nyquist limit is PRF/2; a low scale lowers the Nyquist limit so higher shifts wrap around. Doppler gain changes brightness, not the Nyquist limit.
exam3.hint: Relate the scale control to PRF and the Nyquist limit.

exam3.question: Which index is related to likelihood of cavitation?
exam3.explanation: The mechanical index (peak rarefactional pressure divided by the square root of frequency) estimates the likelihood of cavitation. The thermal index estimates tissue temperature rise.
exam3.hint: Cavitation is a non-thermal effect driven by negative pressure.

exam3.question: Which factor influences color flow imaging frame rate?
exam3.explanation: Higher line density means more scan lines per frame, each requiring a packet of pulses, which lowers frame rate. Filter, dynamic range and map selection are processing choices that do not change pulse timing.
exam3.hint: Frame rate depends on how many pulses must be sent to build each frame.

exam3.question: Which type of resolution will be improved with reducing the depth of field?
exam3.explanation: Shallower depth shortens the listening time per pulse, raising PRF and frame rate, which improves temporal resolution. Axial resolution depends on SPL and is unchanged by depth.
exam3.hint: Think about how imaging depth affects the time needed to build each frame.

exam3.question: Which change improves temporal resolution during color flow imaging?
exam3.explanation: Fewer pulses per packet means less time per color line, which raises color frame rate. Increasing line density or field of view adds more lines and lowers the frame rate.
exam3.hint: Count the pulses sent down each color line.
keywords: temporal resolution during color flow imaging

exam3.question: During a color Doppler scan, which angle to flow would most likely result in no color?
exam3.explanation: Doppler shift is proportional to cos(angle); near 90 degrees cosine approaches zero, so little or no shift and no color is displayed. Angles near 0 or 180 degrees give the largest shifts.
exam3.hint: Think about the value of the cosine as the angle approaches perpendicular.

exam3.question: Penetration can be improved by decreasing which setting?
exam3.explanation: Lower frequency attenuates less, so sound travels deeper and penetration improves. Decreasing output power or gain would make deep echoes weaker.
exam3.hint: Recall how attenuation varies with transducer frequency.

exam3.question: What does a string phantom evaluate?
exam3.explanation: A string phantom uses a moving string at a known speed to test the accuracy of Doppler velocity measurements. Slice thickness and 2D resolution are checked with tissue-mimicking phantoms.
exam3.hint: This device moves a filament at a known speed for Doppler quality assurance.

exam3.question: What affects the gray scale of a 2D image?
exam3.explanation: Dynamic range (compression) sets how many shades of gray are displayed, controlling image contrast. Doppler gain only affects Doppler signals, not the grayscale image.
exam3.hint: Consider which control determines the number of gray shades shown.

exam3.question: What results from increasing the packet length when using color Doppler imaging?
exam3.explanation: More pulses per color line improve sensitivity and accuracy but take more time, so frame rate decreases. Packet length does not change the Nyquist limit, so aliasing is unaffected.
exam3.hint: Longer packets cost time per color scan line.

exam3.question: Which describes the reflected frequency when the reflector is moving towards the sound source?
exam3.explanation: A reflector moving toward the transducer compresses the wave, producing a positive Doppler shift (higher received frequency). A decrease occurs when the reflector moves away.
exam3.hint: Think of a siren approaching you compared with one moving away.

exam3.question: What is the effect of an increased aperture in a linear array transducer?
exam3.explanation: Near zone length increases with aperture squared, so a larger active aperture moves the focus deeper. It lengthens rather than shortens the near field, and axial resolution depends on SPL.
exam3.hint: Recall how near zone length depends on aperture diameter.

exam3.question: Which resolution is improved by focusing?
exam3.explanation: Focusing narrows the beam in the focal region, and lateral resolution equals beam width. Axial resolution depends on pulse length, which focusing does not change.
exam3.hint: Focusing changes the width of the beam.

exam3.question: If the speed of sound in a medium is less than the average speed of sound, where is the reflector positioned?
exam3.explanation: The system assumes 1540 m/s; slower sound takes longer to return, so the system places the reflector deeper than its true position. Faster media make reflectors appear too shallow.
exam3.hint: Remember the range equation assumes 13 microseconds per cm of depth.
keywords: less than the average speed of sound

exam3.question: Which artifact misrepresents direction of flow?
exam3.explanation: When the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit, high velocities wrap to the opposite side of the baseline, falsely suggesting reversed flow. Twinkle is a color artifact behind rough strong reflectors, not a direction error.
exam3.hint: Consider what happens to shifts above the Nyquist limit on the spectral display or color bar.

exam3.question: Which factor has a positive effect on temporal resolution?

options.text: Increase in number of focal zones

exam3.explanation: A narrower sector needs fewer scan lines per frame, raising frame rate. More focal zones, compounding and deeper imaging all lower frame rate.
exam3.hint: Pick the change that reduces the time needed to build one frame.

exam3.question: What causes posterior acoustic enhancement?
exam3.explanation: Structures that attenuate less than surrounding tissue (such as fluid-filled cysts) let more energy reach deeper tissue, brightening it. Strongly attenuating structures cause shadowing instead.
exam3.hint: Compare how much energy is removed by the structure versus the surrounding tissue.

exam3.question: Which of these modes has the highest duty factor?
exam3.explanation: Continuous wave transmits all the time, so its duty factor is 100% (1.0). Pulsed modes transmit only a small fraction of the time and listen the rest.
exam3.hint: Duty factor is the fraction of time the system is transmitting.

exam3.question: Which artifact can be corrected by reducing color gain?
exam3.explanation: Excess color gain makes color spread beyond the vessel wall (blooming), and reducing gain confines it. Aliasing is corrected by raising the scale/PRF or baseline, not gain.
exam3.hint: Think about which artifact makes color spill outside the vessel lumen.

exam3.question: Name 2 types of cavitation in tissue.
exam3.explanation: Stable cavitation involves bubbles that oscillate without bursting, and transient (inertial) cavitation involves bubbles that violently collapse. Thermal and mechanical are the two categories of bioeffects, not types of cavitation.
exam3.hint: One kind of bubble behavior oscillates; the other ends in collapse.

exam3.question: What is the primary determining factor of the fundamental frequency in a pulsed wave transducer?
exam3.explanation: Resonant frequency equals the speed of sound in the element divided by twice its thickness, and thickness is the main design variable: thinner crystals give higher frequency. Crystal diameter affects beam shape, not frequency.
exam3.hint: Recall the half-wavelength rule for piezoelectric elements.

exam3.question: Which adjustment follows the ALARA principle?
exam3.explanation: ALARA means keeping exposure as low as reasonably achievable; reducing output power directly lowers patient exposure, ideally compensated with receiver gain. Depth and sector width do not reduce acoustic exposure.
exam3.hint: Choose the control that changes the energy delivered to the patient.

exam3.question: What causes color flash artifact?
exam3.explanation: Flash artifact is a burst of color from tissue or transducer motion, such as cardiac pulsation or breathing. Aliasing produces color wrap-around within a vessel, not random flashes.
exam3.hint: This artifact appears as a sudden burst of color outside vessels with no real flow.

exam3.question: Which outcome is an advantage of more pulses in an ensemble length?
exam3.explanation: Larger packets give the autocorrelator more samples, improving the accuracy of mean velocity estimates and sensitivity to slow flow. They reduce, not improve, temporal resolution.
exam3.hint: More samples per color line trade time for better estimates.

exam3.question: Which setting will lead to the highest temporal resolution?

options.text: 45 degree sector width, 4 cm scan depth, color Doppler off
60 degree sector width, 5 cm scan depth, color Doppler off
45 degree sector width, 4 cm scan depth, color Doppler on
60 degree sector width, 5 cm scan depth, color Doppler on

exam3.explanation: The narrowest sector, shallowest depth and no color each reduce the time per frame, giving the highest frame rate. Turning color on adds many pulses per line and lowers frame rate.
exam3.hint: Combine every choice that shortens frame time.

exam3.question: Which artifact displays reflectors more shallow than their actual position?
exam3.explanation: With a high PRF, echoes from a deep reflector return after the next pulse is sent and are placed too shallow. Mirror image artifacts are placed deeper than the true structure.
exam3.hint: Consider echoes that arrive after the next pulse has already been transmitted.
keywords: more shallow than their actual position

exam3.question: What happens to the amount of attenuation if the path length is doubled?
exam3.explanation: Total attenuation in dB equals the attenuation coefficient times path length, so doubling distance doubles attenuation. It is a linear, not squared, relationship.
exam3.hint: Attenuation in decibels is coefficient multiplied by distance.

exam3.question: What determines the resonant frequency of a pulsed wave transducer?

options.text: Element thickness and speed of sound in element
Element diameter and speed of sound in element

exam3.explanation: Resonant frequency equals propagation speed in the crystal divided by twice the thickness. Diameter affects beam divergence and focal depth, not operating frequency.
exam3.hint: Recall the formula for resonant frequency of a piezoelectric element.

exam3.question: At which angle to blood flow would the maximum Doppler shift occur?
exam3.explanation: Doppler shift is proportional to cos(theta), and cos 0 = 1, its maximum. At 90 degrees cosine is zero and no shift is detected.
exam3.hint: Find the angle where cosine is largest.

exam3.question: During 3D volume acquisition, the quality of the images is most dependent upon which factor?

options.text: Speed of post processing image compression

exam3.explanation: A 3D volume is built from stacked 2D slices, so the more slices acquired across the volume, the finer the sampling and the better the reconstructed image. Rendering only changes how already-acquired data is displayed.
exam3.hint: Think about how a volume data set is built from individual 2D planes.

exam3.question: If the PRF is 3 kHz, what is the maximum Doppler shift that can be detected without aliasing?
exam3.explanation: The Nyquist limit equals half the PRF, so 3 kHz / 2 = 1.5 kHz is the highest shift measurable without aliasing. Any value at or above the PRF would alias.
exam3.hint: Apply the Nyquist limit relationship to the given PRF.

exam3.question: What is the primary factor that improves lateral resolution?
exam3.explanation: Lateral resolution equals beam width, so a narrower beam (from focusing) directly improves it. Frequency helps mainly by reducing divergence in the far field, an indirect effect.
exam3.hint: Lateral resolution is numerically equal to one beam dimension.

exam3.question: Which factor is improved with spatial compounding?
exam3.explanation: Combining frames acquired from several steering angles reduces speckle and better defines specular boundaries, improving image quality. Because several frames are combined, frame rate decreases.
exam3.hint: Compounding averages views from several beam angles into one frame.

exam3.question: Which unfocused transducer will have the greatest divergence?
exam3.explanation: Beam divergence in the far field increases with smaller aperture and lower frequency, so the 4 mm, 4 MHz transducer diverges most. The 6 mm, 6 MHz transducer diverges least.
exam3.hint: Both a small diameter and a low frequency spread the far-field beam.

exam3.question: What does damping in a pulsed wave transducer affect?
exam3.explanation: Damping reduces the number of cycles in each pulse, shortening pulse duration and SPL. PRF depends on imaging depth, not on damping.
exam3.hint: Damping limits how long the crystal rings after excitation.

exam3.question: Which feature is characteristic of a continuous wave transducer?
exam3.explanation: CW transducers need at least two crystals, one always transmitting and one always receiving. Because they lack range resolution, they have no range specificity, and they do not alias.
exam3.hint: Consider how a probe can send and listen at the same time.

exam3.question: Which artifact results from decreased attenuation?
exam3.explanation: When a structure attenuates less than surrounding tissue, deeper echoes are brighter than expected, creating enhancement. Comet tail and ringdown are reverberation-type artifacts, not attenuation artifacts.
exam3.hint: Compare artifacts caused by too much attenuation with those caused by too little.

exam3.question: Which adjustment will improve axial resolution?
exam3.explanation: Higher frequency shortens wavelength and SPL, and axial resolution equals SPL/2. Gain, dynamic range and output power do not change pulse length.
exam3.hint: Axial resolution depends on spatial pulse length.

exam3.question: What is the term for the ability of an ultrasound system to display low level echoes?
exam3.explanation: Sensitivity is the system's ability to detect and display weak echoes. Resolution terms describe separating closely spaced reflectors, not detecting weak ones.
exam3.hint: This QA parameter concerns weak signals rather than closely spaced ones.

exam3.question: Which artifact causes a reflector to be improperly positioned on the display?
exam3.explanation: Range ambiguity places deep echoes at a shallower depth because they return after the next pulse is sent. Shadowing and enhancement change brightness, not position.
exam3.hint: Look for the artifact that errs in depth placement rather than brightness.

exam3.question: What reduces speckle and increases visualization of specular reflectors and attenuated structures?
exam3.explanation: Spatial compounding averages frames steered at different angles, reducing speckle and improving visualization of curved specular boundaries and areas behind attenuators. Extended field of view enlarges the image but does not reduce speckle.
exam3.hint: Think of combining several beam steering angles into one image.

exam3.question: Which type of structure is best visualized with low persistence?
exam3.explanation: Low persistence averages fewer frames, so rapidly moving (dynamic) structures such as cardiac valves are not blurred. High persistence smooths the image and is suited to static structures.
exam3.hint: Frame averaging blurs anything that moves between frames.

exam3.question: What increases frame rate?

options.text: Increase the number of lines per frame
Decrease the number of focal zones

exam3.explanation: Each focal zone requires a separate pulse per line, so fewer focal zones shorten frame time and raise frame rate. Wider sectors and more lines per frame lower frame rate.
exam3.hint: Count the pulses needed per scan line.

exam3.question: What happens when the PRF is less than twice the Doppler shift frequency?
exam3.explanation: If PRF is below twice the Doppler shift, the shift exceeds the Nyquist limit and aliasing occurs. Range ambiguity is a depth-placement artifact from very high PRF.
exam3.hint: Relate PRF to the Nyquist limit.
keywords: less than twice the Doppler shift frequency

exam3.question: Which resolution capability is most affected by SPL?
exam3.explanation: Axial resolution equals SPL/2, so shorter pulses resolve reflectors closer together along the beam. Lateral and elevational resolution depend on beam width.
exam3.hint: Think about the resolution measured along the direction of the beam.

exam3.question: What control changes contrast resolution?
exam3.explanation: Dynamic range (compression) sets the number of gray shades displayed, directly controlling contrast resolution. Gain brightens all echoes uniformly without changing gray-scale differentiation.
exam3.hint: Contrast resolution is about how many shades of gray are available.

exam3.question: The ability to resolve 2 separate reflectors perpendicular to the path of the beam is which resolution?
exam3.explanation: Lateral resolution distinguishes side-by-side reflectors perpendicular to the beam and equals beam width. Axial resolution applies to reflectors parallel to the beam path.
exam3.hint: Separate the resolution along the beam from the one across it.
keywords: perpendicular to the path of the beam

exam3.question: Which type of display rescans only the region of interest and improves visualization?
exam3.explanation: Write (preprocessing) zoom rescans only the region of interest with more scan lines and pixels, improving spatial resolution. Read zoom enlarges stored data without adding detail.
exam3.hint: Distinguish preprocessing zoom from postprocessing zoom.
keywords: rescans only the region of interest

exam3.question: Which color Doppler setting can be optimized to eliminate low Doppler frequency shifts?
exam3.explanation: The wall filter is a high-pass filter that removes low-frequency shifts from wall motion and slow tissue. Scale sets the PRF and Nyquist limit; although raising scale may raise the filter on some systems, it is not the control designed for this.
exam3.hint: Low-frequency shifts come mainly from vessel walls and slow tissue motion; think of the control built to reject them.

exam3.question: Which statement describes the purpose of using a spectral Doppler wall filter?

options.text: To clean up the audio signal
To widen the area in which the Doppler shift is sampled

exam3.explanation: The wall filter rejects low-frequency (low velocity), high-amplitude signals from vessel walls and tissue motion. It does not affect high velocities or sample volume size.
exam3.hint: Think about what kind of signal moving vessel walls produce.

exam3.question: What is the primary reason to use compression?
exam3.explanation: Compression reduces the wide range of echo amplitudes to a range the display can show, adjusting the gray-scale (contrast). It does not change pulse length or scan lines.
exam3.hint: Compression maps a large range of signal strengths onto fewer gray shades.

exam3.question: What is affected by increasing color scale?
exam3.explanation: The color scale sets PRF, and the Nyquist limit is PRF/2, so increasing scale raises the Nyquist limit and reduces aliasing. Color priority is an independent control that decides whether color or gray scale is displayed at a pixel.
exam3.hint: Relate the scale control to PRF.

exam3.question: What happens when a sound wave encounters a smooth flat surface?
exam3.explanation: A smooth, flat boundary larger than the wavelength produces specular reflection. Diffraction is spreading of the wave, not its return from a surface.
exam3.hint: Think of the reflection type from mirror-like boundaries.

exam3.question: Which method of sanitizing the transducer will damage the PZT?
exam3.explanation: Autoclaving uses high heat, which can exceed the Curie temperature and depolarize the PZT crystal, destroying its piezoelectric properties. Glutaraldehyde is an approved high-level disinfectant for many probes.
exam3.hint: Recall what happens to PZT above its Curie point.

exam3.question: What is the most effective way to reduce aliasing on color Doppler?
exam3.explanation: Raising PRF (scale) raises the Nyquist limit so higher Doppler shifts can be displayed without wrap-around. Decreasing PRF lowers the Nyquist limit and worsens aliasing.
exam3.hint: Aliasing occurs when the shift exceeds half the PRF.

exam3.question: What is an advantage of power Doppler over color Doppler?
exam3.explanation: Power Doppler displays the amplitude (strength) of the Doppler signal, making it more sensitive to slow flow and relatively angle independent. It provides no velocity or direction information and is more prone to flash artifact.
exam3.hint: Power Doppler encodes signal strength rather than frequency shift.

exam3.question: What is the function of M-mode?
exam3.explanation: M-mode displays reflector depth over time along one scan line, used to measure motion such as valve and wall movement. Blood flow is evaluated with Doppler.
exam3.hint: Consider what M-mode plots on its vertical axis versus its horizontal time axis.

exam3.question: Which change can be made to avoid exceeding the Nyquist limit?
exam3.explanation: The Nyquist limit equals PRF/2, so increasing PRF raises the limit and prevents aliasing. Output power has no effect on the Nyquist limit.
exam3.hint: Recall how the Nyquist limit is calculated.

exam3.question: A Doppler shift is 10,000 Hz at an angle to flow of 60 degrees. What is the Doppler shift at 0 degrees?
exam3.explanation: Doppler shift is proportional to cos(theta); cos 60 = 0.5 and cos 0 = 1, so the shift doubles to 20,000 Hz. 5,000 Hz would result from incorrectly multiplying by 0.5.
exam3.hint: Compare the cosine of 60 degrees with the cosine of 0 degrees.

exam3.question: According to Poiseuille's law, a change in which parameter would have the greatest influence on blood flow?
exam3.explanation: In Poiseuille's law, flow is proportional to radius to the fourth power, so small radius changes have huge effects. Pressure gradient, length and viscosity affect flow only linearly.
exam3.hint: Look for the variable raised to a power in the equation.

exam3.question: Which system control adjusts amplification of signal as a function of depth?
exam3.explanation: Time gain compensation amplifies echoes according to their arrival time (depth) to compensate for attenuation. Output power changes all echoes equally by changing the transmitted pulse.
exam3.hint: Think of the control that compensates for attenuation with depth.

exam3.question: Which factor affects temporal resolution?
exam3.explanation: Display depth determines the listening time per pulse and thus frame rate and temporal resolution. Compression, gain and TGC are receiver processing functions that do not change frame rate.
exam3.hint: Choose the control that changes the time needed for each pulse-echo cycle.

exam3.question: What happens to the Doppler shift when the angle is changed from 30 to 60 degrees?
exam3.explanation: Cosine falls from about 0.87 at 30 degrees to 0.5 at 60 degrees, so the Doppler shift decreases. A complete loss of signal would occur only near 90 degrees.
exam3.hint: Compare the cosine values of the two angles.

exam4.question: Which adjustment would reduce the artifact seen along the baseline of this spectral Doppler tracing?
exam4.explanation: Clutter (wall thump) is low-velocity, high-amplitude Doppler signal from moving vessel walls or tissue, displayed close to the baseline. The wall filter is a high-pass filter that rejects these low-frequency shifts; it should be set high enough to remove clutter without discarding real low-velocity flow.
exam4.hint: The unwanted signal is low in frequency shift but strong in amplitude, so a high-pass filter can reject it.
exam4.imageCaption: Spectral Doppler tracing

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated by the color appearing in the tissue next to the vessel wall at the arrow?
exam4.explanation: Ghosting is clutter in color Doppler: pulsating vessel walls and surrounding tissue move slowly but reflect strongly, creating low-frequency Doppler shifts that are color-encoded outside the lumen. Raising the color wall filter removes these low-velocity, high-amplitude signals.
exam4.hint: Moving vessel walls and adjacent tissue produce strong, low-velocity Doppler shifts that the system can paint as flow.
exam4.imageCaption: Longitudinal color Doppler image of a vessel

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this color Doppler image?
exam4.explanation: Aliasing occurs when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit (one-half the PRF). In color Doppler the fastest flow wraps to the opposite end of the color bar, so the reverse color appears directly next to the brightest forward color with no black band between them.
exam4.hint: Compare the flow speed with the low velocity limit on the color bar; mid-lumen color jumps from one end of the bar to the other.
exam4.imageCaption: Longitudinal color Doppler image of an artery

exam4.question: Which adjustment would reduce the artifact seen in this image?
exam4.explanation: Aliasing appears when the Doppler shift exceeds the Nyquist limit, which equals half the PRF. Raising the scale raises the PRF and therefore the Nyquist limit; shifting the baseline, using a lower transducer frequency, or a shallower depth also help, whereas a higher frequency would increase the Doppler shift and worsen it.
exam4.hint: The Nyquist limit equals one-half of the pulse repetition frequency.
exam4.imageCaption: Color Doppler image of a vessel

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this pulsed wave Doppler spectrum?
exam4.explanation: The systolic peaks exceed the Nyquist limit (half the PRF), so their tops are cut off and wrap around to appear below the baseline. Increasing the scale (PRF), lowering the baseline, using a lower-frequency transducer, or switching to continuous wave Doppler eliminates it.
exam4.hint: The peaks are clipped at the top of the scale and reappear from the bottom edge of the display.
exam4.imageCaption: Pulsed wave Doppler spectrum

exam4.question: Which adjustment would reduce the artifact seen in this spectral Doppler display?

options.text: Reposition the transducer so the insonation angle is not near 90 degrees

exam4.explanation: Spectral mirroring (crosstalk) shows a weaker copy of the spectrum on the opposite side of the baseline. It occurs when the beam meets flow at or near 90 degrees, so the receiver detects shifts in both directions, and it is worsened by excessive Doppler gain; reducing the angle or lowering the gain removes it.
exam4.hint: The copy is strongest when the beam strikes flow nearly perpendicular, so the receiver cannot sort out flow direction.
exam4.imageCaption: Spectral Doppler display

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this grayscale image?
exam4.explanation: A strong specular reflector redirects the beam to an object and back along the same path, but the system assumes straight-line travel and places a copy deeper than the reflector. The real structure lies closer to the transducer; the copy is always on the far side of the reflector.
exam4.hint: A duplicate lies an equal distance on the far side of a bright, curved interface.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale abdominal image

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this color Doppler image of the subclavian region?
exam4.explanation: The bright pleural line is a strong specular reflector, so color flow from the subclavian vessel is reflected and displayed a second time deep to the reflector. Mirror artifacts can appear on grayscale, color, and spectral Doppler.
exam4.hint: The copy of the flow lies directly deep to a highly reflective line, as far below it as the real vessel lies above.
exam4.imageCaption: Color Doppler image of the subclavian region

exam4.question: Which artifact explains the liver-like tissue displayed beyond the diaphragm in this image?
exam4.explanation: The diaphragm-lung interface is a strong specular reflector: sound reflects off it into the liver and returns along the same route. Because the system assumes straight-line travel, it displays liver tissue beyond the diaphragm, where aerated lung should appear dark.
exam4.hint: Aerated lung should not show solid tissue texture, and the diaphragm is a highly reflective curved interface.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the liver and right kidney

exam4.question: Which adjustment would reduce the artifact seen in this image?
exam4.explanation: Blooming happens when color gain is set too high, so color spills past the vessel walls and random color speckles appear in the surrounding tissue. Lowering the color gain keeps color inside the lumen.
exam4.hint: Color is spilling into stationary tissue because the receiver is boosting weak signals too much.
exam4.imageCaption: Longitudinal color Doppler image of an artery

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated by the low-level echoes at the arrow within this urinary bladder?
exam4.explanation: The beam has finite thickness in the elevational plane, so echoes from tissue just outside the scan plane are averaged into the anechoic bladder and mimic sludge or debris. It is reduced by narrowing the elevational beam (1.5-D or 2-D arrays, elevational focusing) and with harmonic imaging; TGC does not remove it.
exam4.hint: The beam is not infinitely thin; it also has width perpendicular to the image plane.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the urinary bladder

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated by the mosaic color signal behind the echogenic focus in this color Doppler image?
exam4.explanation: Twinkle artifact is a rapidly changing mixture of colors behind a strongly reflecting, rough surface such as a renal stone. It comes from phase jitter (narrow-band noise) produced at the rough interface and is a useful sign of a calculus even when shadowing is weak.
exam4.hint: The signal sits deep to a rough, highly reflective stone and does not follow any vessel.
exam4.imageCaption: Color Doppler image of the kidney

exam4.question: Which adjustment would reduce the artifact seen in this image?
exam4.explanation: Side lobes are weak off-axis beams; strong reflectors they strike are displayed as if on the main axis, placing false echoes inside an anechoic cyst. Harmonic signals form mainly in the strong central beam, so harmonic imaging suppresses side lobe artifacts; apodization does the same at the transducer.
exam4.hint: The false echo comes from weak off-axis energy, which generates very little second-harmonic signal.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of an anechoic cyst

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated deep to the echogenic foci in this image?
exam4.explanation: Gallstones attenuate sound strongly by reflection and absorption, so little energy reaches deeper tissue and the region beneath appears dark. Shadowing results from high attenuation, the opposite of enhancement.
exam4.hint: The structures above the dark band reflect and absorb most of the beam.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the gallbladder

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated at the arrow, deep to the fluid-filled structure in this image?
exam4.explanation: Fluid attenuates less than the surrounding soft tissue, but TGC compensates for average tissue attenuation, so echoes behind the fluid are over-amplified and appear brighter. Enhancement results from abnormally low attenuation.
exam4.hint: The beam crossing the fluid loses less energy than beams crossing soft tissue at the same depth.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the liver and gallbladder

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated by the horizontal band of increased brightness at one depth in this image?
exam4.explanation: Intensity is highest at the focus, where the beam is narrowest, so tissue at the focal depth appears brighter than tissue above and below it. Adjusting TGC or using multiple focal zones evens out the brightness.
exam4.hint: Check where the focal zone is set relative to the bright band.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the liver

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated at the arrow in this image?
exam4.explanation: Sound bounces back and forth between two strong parallel reflectors, or between a reflector and the transducer. Each extra round trip takes more time, so the system displays equally spaced, progressively weaker echoes deeper than the real one.
exam4.hint: The extra lines are equally spaced along the beam, each representing another round trip.
exam4.imageCaption: Parasternal echocardiographic image

exam4.question: Which artifact produces the multiple, equally spaced parallel lines deep to the needle in this image?
exam4.explanation: The beam bounces between the front and back walls of the metal needle, a pair of strong reflectors close together. Each additional round trip arrives later and is displayed as another line deeper and parallel to the needle.
exam4.hint: A metal shaft has two strong reflecting walls close together.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image during needle guidance

exam4.question: Which artifact is indicated by the arrows in this lung image?
exam4.explanation: Comet tail is a form of reverberation in which reflections from a small, very strong reflector are so closely spaced that they merge into a single tapering bright line. The individual echoes are too close together to be resolved separately.
exam4.hint: Very small, highly reflective interfaces create reflections so closely spaced that they fuse into one tapering streak.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale image of the lung base

exam4.question: Which artifact is indicated by the arrows in this image?
exam4.explanation: Ring-down arises when the beam strikes a small collection of gas bubbles; fluid trapped between them resonates and emits sound continuously, producing a solid bright streak that extends deep from the gas. It indicates air rather than a solid reflector.
exam4.hint: Air bubbles with trapped fluid between them can vibrate and keep emitting sound.
exam4.imageCaption: Grayscale abdominal image

exam4.question: Which artifact explains the two identical structures displayed next to each other at the same depth in this image?
exam4.explanation: When the beam crosses an interface between media with different propagation speeds at an oblique angle, it bends (Snell's law). The system assumes a straight path, so one structure is displayed twice, side by side at the same depth; changing the transducer angle or position shows the true anatomy.
exam4.hint: The dashed line traces the bent beam path compared with the assumed straight path.
exam4.imageCaption: Transverse grayscale image of the abdomen

exam4.question: The asterisks mark the rectus abdominis muscles. Which artifact explains the duplicated structure at the arrows?
exam4.explanation: Sound bends at the oblique muscle-fat interfaces of the rectus abdominis because the propagation speeds differ. The bent beam reaches the same deep structure along two paths, and since the system assumes straight-line travel, one structure is displayed twice side by side.
exam4.hint: The muscle-fat interface near the midline lies at an angle, and the two tissues have different propagation speeds.
exam4.imageCaption: Transverse midline abdominal image

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this image?
exam4.explanation: Electrical interference from nearby equipment or poor grounding adds a regular, repeating pattern of dots or lines with no anatomic basis. It is reduced by removing the source or improving grounding, and it differs from speckle, the granular pattern produced by interference of the sound waves themselves.
exam4.hint: The pattern is too regular and evenly spaced to come from tissue scatterers.
exam4.imageCaption: Transesophageal echocardiographic image

exam4.question: Which artifact is demonstrated in this power Doppler image?
exam4.explanation: Flash artifact is a sudden burst of color across the image caused by motion of tissue or the transducer, such as breathing, cardiac pulsation, or patient movement. Power Doppler is especially prone because it is very sensitive and has poor temporal resolution.
exam4.hint: Power Doppler is sensitive enough to pick up motion of the tissue itself.
exam4.imageCaption: Power Doppler image

practice.question: What is the typical frequency range used in diagnostic medical ultrasound?
practice.explanation: Diagnostic medical ultrasound typically uses frequencies between 2 MHz and 15 MHz. Lower frequencies (2-5 MHz) provide better penetration for deeper structures, while higher frequencies (7-15 MHz) provide better resolution for superficial structures.
practice.hint: Medical ultrasound uses MHz (megahertz) frequencies - much higher than human hearing but not as high as some specialized applications.

practice.question: Which of the following best describes the piezoelectric effect?

options.text: Conversion between electrical and mechanical energy
Reflection of sound waves at tissue interfaces
Attenuation of ultrasound beams in tissue

practice.explanation: Piezoelectric materials convert between mechanical and electrical energy: returning echoes deform the crystal and create a voltage (piezoelectric effect), while an applied voltage makes the crystal vibrate and produce sound (reverse piezoelectric effect). Reflection, attenuation and Doppler shift are wave-tissue interactions, not properties of the crystal.
practice.hint: This is the fundamental principle that allows transducers to both create and detect ultrasound waves.

practice.question: What happens to spatial resolution as frequency increases?
practice.explanation: Higher frequencies provide better spatial resolution because they produce shorter wavelengths. However, this comes at the cost of reduced penetration depth due to increased attenuation.
practice.hint: Remember: higher frequency = better resolution but less penetration.

practice.question: Which artifact occurs when the ultrasound beam encounters a strong reflector, causing multiple echoes?
practice.explanation: Reverberation artifact occurs when ultrasound encounters a strong reflector and bounces back and forth between the transducer and the reflector multiple times, creating equally spaced parallel echoes.
practice.hint: Think about what happens when sound bounces back and forth repeatedly - like an echo that echoes.

practice.question: What is the relationship between frequency and wavelength in ultrasound?
practice.explanation: Frequency and wavelength are inversely proportional. As frequency increases, wavelength decreases. This relationship is described by the equation: wavelength = propagation speed / frequency.
practice.hint: Remember: higher frequency = better resolution but less penetration.

practice.question: What is the average propagation speed of ultrasound in soft tissue?
practice.explanation: The average propagation speed of ultrasound in soft tissue is 1,540 m/s (or 1.54 mm/µs). This value is used by ultrasound machines to calculate distance and is the basis for accurate imaging.
practice.hint: Apply fundamental ultrasound physics principles.

practice.question: What control adjusts the brightness of echoes returning from deeper structures?
practice.explanation: Time Gain Compensation (TGC) selectively amplifies echoes returning from deeper structures to compensate for attenuation. This creates a more uniform image brightness at all depths.
practice.hint: Deeper echoes are weaker because of attenuation, so look for the control that amplifies selectively by depth rather than uniformly.

practice.question: Which type of resolution refers to the ability to distinguish two structures lying perpendicular to the beam?
practice.explanation: Lateral resolution (also called azimuthal resolution) is the ability to distinguish two structures that are side-by-side, perpendicular to the ultrasound beam. It is determined by beam width.
practice.hint: Lateral = side-to-side, perpendicular to the beam. Axial = along the beam.

practice.question: What does the Doppler effect measure in ultrasound?
practice.explanation: The Doppler effect measures the frequency shift that occurs when ultrasound reflects off moving structures (typically blood cells). This shift is proportional to the velocity of the moving target and is used to assess blood flow.
practice.hint: Doppler measures the frequency change when ultrasound bounces off moving blood - higher/lower pitch indicates direction and speed.

practice.question: What is acoustic impedance?

options.text: The resistance of tissue to ultrasound propagation
The speed of sound in tissue
The frequency of the ultrasound beam
The power output of the transducer

practice.explanation: Acoustic impedance is the resistance that tissue offers to the propagation of ultrasound. It is the product of tissue density and the speed of sound in that tissue. Differences in acoustic impedance between tissues create reflections.
practice.hint: Acoustic impedance = tissue density × sound speed. Differences in impedance create reflections at tissue boundaries.

practice.question: What artifact appears as an anechoic shadow behind highly attenuating structures?
practice.explanation: Acoustic shadowing appears as a dark (anechoic) area behind structures that strongly attenuate or reflect ultrasound, such as bone, calcifications, or gallstones. This occurs because little to no sound energy passes through to deeper structures.
practice.hint: Shadowing = dark area behind highly attenuating structures like bone, stones, or calcifications.

practice.question: Which transducer type produces a rectangular image format?
practice.explanation: Linear array transducers produce a rectangular image format with uniform width throughout the image. They are commonly used for vascular imaging, musculoskeletal imaging, and small parts.
practice.hint: Linear = rectangular image. Sector/phased = fan-shaped. Curved = curved/trapezoidal.

practice.question: What happens to penetration as frequency increases?
practice.explanation: As frequency increases, penetration decreases. Higher frequency sound waves are attenuated more rapidly in tissue, limiting their ability to penetrate deeply. This is why lower frequencies are used for imaging deeper structures.
practice.hint: Higher frequency = better resolution BUT less penetration. Lower frequency = worse resolution BUT more penetration.

practice.question: What does the overall gain control adjust?

options.text: Brightness of the entire image uniformly

practice.explanation: Overall gain adjusts the amplification of all returning echoes uniformly, affecting the brightness of the entire image equally at all depths. This is different from TGC, which selectively adjusts gain at different depths.
practice.hint: Overall gain = uniform brightness adjustment everywhere. TGC = depth-specific brightness adjustment.

practice.question: What is the primary advantage of harmonic imaging?

options.text: Improved image quality and reduced artifacts

practice.explanation: Harmonic imaging uses frequency components generated within tissue (usually at twice the transmitted frequency). This technique reduces artifacts, improves contrast resolution, and produces cleaner images, especially in difficult-to-image patients.
practice.hint: Harmonics are generated within tissue rather than at the skin surface, so they avoid much of the near-field clutter and side-lobe artifact.

practice.question: What is the optimal Doppler angle for accurate velocity measurements?
practice.explanation: The Doppler shift is proportional to the cosine of the beam-to-flow angle, so 0 degrees gives the largest shift and the smallest velocity error from angle misestimation. In clinical vascular work, angles of 60 degrees or less are accepted because errors grow rapidly above 60 degrees, and at 90 degrees no shift is detected.
practice.hint: Best Doppler angle is 45-60°. At 90° there's NO Doppler shift. Keep angle <60° for accurate velocities.

practice.question: What causes aliasing in pulsed wave Doppler?
practice.explanation: Aliasing occurs when the velocity of blood flow exceeds the Nyquist limit (half the pulse repetition frequency). This causes the Doppler waveform to wrap around and appear on the opposite side of the baseline, creating ambiguous velocity information.
practice.hint: Aliasing = velocity too fast for the PRF setting. Waveform wraps around and appears on wrong side of baseline.

practice.question: Which artifact appears as bright echoes behind fluid-filled structures?
practice.explanation: Acoustic enhancement (also called through-transmission) appears as increased echogenicity (brightness) behind fluid-filled structures. This occurs because fluid attenuates sound less than surrounding tissue, allowing more energy to reach deeper structures.
practice.hint: Enhancement = bright area behind fluid (cysts, bladder). Fluid transmits sound better than solid tissue.

practice.question: What is the mechanical index (MI) used to assess?
practice.explanation: The Mechanical Index (MI) is used to assess the potential for non-thermal bioeffects, specifically cavitation. Cavitation is the formation and collapse of gas bubbles in tissue due to the mechanical pressure of ultrasound waves.
practice.hint: MI = Mechanical Index = cavitation risk (bubble formation). TI = Thermal Index = heating risk.

practice.question: What is axial resolution dependent upon?
practice.explanation: Axial resolution (also called longitudinal or range resolution) is the ability to distinguish two structures along the beam axis. It is determined by spatial pulse length - shorter pulses (fewer cycles, higher frequency) provide better axial resolution.
practice.hint: Axial resolution depends on pulse length. Shorter pulse = better axial resolution. Higher frequency helps!
